title: Grace Hopper's nanosecond
hook: A computer pioneer handed out bits of wire to show what a billionth of a second is.
peek: Grace Hopper, the US Navy computer scientist, carried lengths of wire about 30 centimetres long. Each was a nanosecond: the distance light travels in a billionth of a second. It made an invisible delay something you could hold.
lede: Grace Hopper helped program some of the first computers and pushed for programming languages written in words. She also had a gift for explaining them. When admirals asked why messages via satellite took so long, she handed them a piece of wire 11.8 inches long, about 30 centimetres. That, she said, was a nanosecond: as far as light can go in a billionth of a second.

bullets.text: Light covers about 300,000 kilometres a second, so in a billionth of a second it gets just under 30 centimetres. A satellite tens of thousands of kilometres up is a great many of Hopper's wires away, and each one costs time.
The wire stood for light in empty space. Real signals moving through a cable travel somewhat slower, often around two thirds as fast, so the true nanosecond of a computer wire is shorter still.
She also showed a coil of wire about 300 metres long, roughly 984 feet: a microsecond, a thousand nanoseconds. She used it to argue that programmers should not waste even a millionth of a second.

For a picosecond, a thousandth of a nanosecond, she is said to have handed out grains of pepper, a length far too short to cut from wire. She kept giving out nanoseconds in talks for decades, including on television in the 1980s.
